name: Topical melatonin hair
lead: Topical melatonin for hair refers to melatonin solutions applied to the scalp by people with androgenetic alopecia who hope to slow thinning and thicken hair, usually alongside established treatments. Melatonin is a hormone made mainly by the pineal gland that regulates sleep-wake timing, and it is also an in vitro antioxidant.[1]

Interest in the scalp comes from the idea that hair follicles are themselves sites of melatonin activity and that its antioxidant properties could protect them; proponents point to this reasoning, while reviews describe the hair evidence as varying in strength.[1][3] Wikipedia's article on pattern hair loss lists topical melatonin among androgen-independent treatments, alongside the established options of minoxidil, finasteride, dutasteride, hair transplantation and low-level laser therapy.[5]

A 2026 systematic review with network meta-analysis of off-label androgenetic alopecia therapies reported that topical melatonin was among those that appeared effective for male pattern loss on 6-month change in hair density, with topical 5% minoxidil ranked most effective and the authors calling for higher-quality comparative trials.[2] A 2026 case series has also described topical melatonin in people with hair graying.[4]
infobox: Among off-label topicals that appeared effective at 6 months (2026)[2]

paras: Pattern hair loss is the most common cause of hair loss; by age 50 about half of men and a quarter of women are affected, according to Wikipedia.[5] It results from genetic sensitivity to androgens, mainly dihydrotestosterone formed by 5-alpha-reductase in the scalp, which shrinks follicles over time (miniaturisation); the article also mentions possible roles for oxidative stress, the scalp microbiome and Wnt signalling as less established factors.[5] The oxidative stress idea is the reasoning proponents give for trying an antioxidant like melatonin on the scalp.

Melatonin acts as an agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors and, in vitro, scavenges free radicals and promotes antioxidant enzyme expression.[1] Proponents of scalp use point to these antioxidant properties; whether they translate to hair growth is a question for clinical trials.

A 2026 systematic review with network meta-analyses covering 23 studies, 15 of them off-label therapies, reported that topical melatonin appeared effective for male androgenetic alopecia based on mean 6-month change in total hair density; topical minoxidil 5% ranked highest, and the authors called for higher-quality comparative trials.[2] A 2026 clinical dermatology review names androgenetic alopecia as an area of interest for topical melatonin and says the strength of evidence varies across indications.[3] A 2026 case series examined topical melatonin for hair graying repigmentation.[4] Other 2025 to 2026 network meta-analyses of conventional and non-conventional over-the-counter treatments for male androgenetic alopecia, and reviews of melatonin in dermatology and of the cutaneous melatoninergic system, appear in the literature listing.[6]

Topical melatonin is mentioned in hair-loss communities as an inexpensive add-on to established treatments such as minoxidil. Evidence cited in these discussions tends to be the general pharmacology of melatonin and the small published datasets above.[1][2]

Melatonin is sold over the counter as an oral supplement in many countries, and scalp solutions are marketed by cosmetic and compounding suppliers; no regulator-approved hair-loss indication for topical melatonin was identified.[1] Researchers who published a 2026 review of cutaneous melatonin biology place it within a wider interest in using topical melatonin for photoprotection and skin rejuvenation as well as hair.[3][6]

timeline.event: Melatonin first isolated by the team of Aaron B. Lerner.[1]
Network meta-analysis lists topical melatonin among off-label topicals that appeared effective at 6 months, below minoxidil.[2]

claims.claim: Melatonin on the scalp helps hair growth as an add-on to other treatments
claims.believers: Proponents point to melatonin's antioxidant properties and see it as a low-cost addition to minoxidil-style routines [1].
claims.experts: A 2026 network meta-analysis ranked it among effective off-label topicals but below topical minoxidil, and reviewers call for higher-quality trials [2][3].

card.summary: Melatonin solution on the scalp for androgenetic alopecia: a small-trial idea, not an established treatment.
card.note: Evidence base not confirmed in this entry; check primary trials.

quick.overview:
Melatonin is the sleep-timing hormone; some hair-loss users apply it as a scalp solution.
This entry found general pharmacology only and no loaded trial data, so no effectiveness conclusion is stated.
quick.mechanism: Melatonin acts on MT1/MT2 receptors and has antioxidant effects in vitro; its role in hair follicles is not well documented.
quick.risks: Melatonin is sold over the counter as a supplement in many countries; scalp-specific safety data were not reviewed.

chain: Melatonin solution applied to the scalp
angle.text: Users apply melatonin to thinning scalp areas as an add-on to established hair-loss treatments to try to keep or increase hair density. A 2026 network meta-analysis lists it among off-label topicals that appeared effective on hair density.
